summary.short: Adds 17 U.S.C. § 514 to the Copyright Act, letting owners of exclusive copyrights, or their authorized agents, ask a district court clerk to issue subpoenas requiring AI developers to disclose copies of, or records identifying, copyrighted works used to train generative AI models. Takes effect on enactment.
summary.long: Section 1 gives the short title 'TRAIN Act'. Section 2 adds 17 U.S.C. § 514 to Chapter 5 of the Copyright Act and amends the chapter's table of sections. Section 514 defines artificial intelligence, artificial intelligence model, developer, generative artificial intelligence model, substantially modify and training material. A developer is a person or State or local government agency that designs, produces, owns or substantially modifies a generative model and engages in or supervises training dataset curation or training; noncommercial end users are excluded. An owner of an exclusive copyright right, or an authorized person, may request a clerk of any U.S. district court to issue a subpoena to a developer for copies of, or records identifying, works owned or controlled by that owner used in training, if the requester holds a subjective good faith belief of such use. The request consists of a proposed subpoena and a sworn declaration. If both are in proper form and properly executed, the clerk must expeditiously issue and sign the subpoena. The developer must expeditiously disclose the requested material. Requesters may not disclose the material to others without authorization. Issuance, delivery and remedies follow the Federal Rules of Civil Procedure, as far as practicable. Non-compliance creates a rebuttable presumption that the developer made copies of the copyrighted work. On motion by a recipient, a court may sanction a requester who makes a bad-faith request under Rule 11(c). The section takes effect on the date of enactment.

notes: Introduced text (IH) dated 2026-01-22; registry status is pending. The bill's operative change is one new section, 17 U.S.C. 514, plus a conforming table-of-sections entry. Its 'developer' definition covers State or local government agencies, not only private firms. The only consequences stated for non-compliance are a rebuttable presumption (subsection (i)) and court sanctions for bad-faith requests (subsection (j)). The effective date is the date of enactment (subsection (k)). The Title 17 target is not in the registry, so target_instrument_id is empty.

thresholds.note: The bill sets no numeric cutoff that changes legal treatment. Its numbers are citations (15 U.S.C. 9401, 17 U.S.C. chapter 5, section 514, section 5002) and the phrase '1 or more' copyrighted works, which describes the works a request may cover rather than a threshold. The subpoena, confidentiality, presumption and sanctions provisions (new 17 U.S.C. 514(b) to (j)) contain no numeric trigger.
